title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 61–62
description: Curated B2 time linkers, simultaneous-event expressions, conditions, hypothetical questions and -ever clauses, with context, register and usage contrasts.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow the relevant teaching and exercise topics; teaching examples and explanatory notes are newly written, without reproducing original exercises, extended passages or illustrations.

audit.scope: Full unit study pages, usage notes, illustrations and diagrams, exercises 61.1–61.4 and 62.1–62.4, and associated answer-key entries inspected for vocabulary and usage coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is supplied where confident; longer expressions may omit IPA rather than provide an unreliable transcription. Optional variants and connected-speech detail are not exhaustive.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared target expressions and usage distinctions with the teaching and exercise pages and answer key; reviewed examples, Brazilian Portuguese meanings, source attribution, structure, stable IDs and audio-target suitability. Browser-based TTS, speech recognition and VocabLab import were not tested.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio files; browser voice, pronunciation and speech-recognition behaviour remain dependent on the user environment. No live application import or runtime validation was performed.

units.title: Unit 61 — Time: connecting words and expressions
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 128–129 (PDF pages 129–130).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose accurate expressions for events that happen before, during and after another event.
Distinguish during from throughout, and simultaneous events from events in sequence.
Use stronger or more formal time linkers in appropriate speaking and writing contexts.
Use time clauses and expressions for precise, approximate and non-specific times.

items.example: Prior to starting the experiment, we checked the sensors.
items.note: Formal, particularly in writing; followed by a noun or an -ing form.

items.example: I had previously worked with a different control system.
items.note: Fairly formal; refers to a time before the event or state being discussed.

items.example: We moved to Bristol last year; before that, we lived in Leeds.
items.note: A more conversational alternative to previously when referring back to an earlier time.

items.example: I was busy earlier on, but I can talk now.
items.note: Fairly informal; often used for an earlier part of the same day or period.

items.example: The building was formerly used as a research laboratory.
items.note: Fairly formal and often written; highlights an earlier name, role or state that has changed.

items.example: The replacement part will arrive tomorrow; in the meantime, we can review the drawings.
items.note: Refers to the period before another event occurs or an activity is completed.

items.example: The technician updated the software; meanwhile, I checked the wiring.
items.note: Connects activities or situations taking place during the same broad period.

items.example: The power failed at the very time we were saving the results.
items.note: Stronger and more precise than as; the following clause identifies the coinciding event.

items.example: The alarm sounded at the very moment the test began.
items.note: Emphasises an exact moment when two events coincided; at may be omitted in some contexts.

items.example: As I opened the door, the telephone rang.
items.note: Here as means when or while; it is not the reason-giving use of as.

items.pt: exatamente quando; bem na hora em que
items.example: Just as the meeting started, the projector stopped working.
items.note: Adds emphasis to the precise coincidence of events.

items.example: Both motors must start simultaneously to avoid a sudden load change.
items.note: The actions happen at exactly the same time, rather than merely within the same period.

items.example: Several questions came up during the workshop.
items.note: Preposition + noun or noun phrase; the action may occupy only part of the named period.

items.pt: durante todo; ao longo de todo
items.example: The monitoring system remained active throughout the night.
items.note: Covers the entire period from beginning to end; contrasts with during.

items.example: Two operators noticed the fault at the same time.
items.note: General way to describe simultaneous actions; simultaneously is often more formal.

items.example: Following the inspection, the equipment was returned to service.
items.note: Formal preposition in this use; takes a noun phrase, not a finite clause.

items.example: We reviewed the measurements and subsequently adjusted the controller.
items.note: Rather formal; means at some point after an event, without necessarily meaning immediately.

items.pt: a partir de então; depois disso
items.example: The team completed training in June and worked independently thereafter.
items.note: Rather formal, often written; means after the event or time just mentioned.

items.example: The software update had an immediate effect on performance.
items.note: An adjective for an effect or response occurring at once; compare subsequently.

items.pt: assim que; no instante em que
items.example: The moment the sensor detects a problem, the system stops.
items.note: Introduces a time clause meaning as soon as; no preposition is needed before the clause.

items.pt: assim que; no minuto em que
items.example: The minute I received the confirmation, I informed the team.
items.note: Conversational alternative to the moment, meaning as soon as.

items.pt: na ocasião em que; na vez em que
items.example: I remember the time that we first demonstrated the prototype.
items.note: Refers to a particular occasion; that can often be omitted.

items.example: I met the director twice, but on that occasion we only discussed the schedule.
items.note: More formal than that time; refers back to one specific occasion.

items.example: We encountered a similar warning on several occasions last month.
items.note: A rather formal way to say several times.

items.pt: em uma etapa posterior; mais adiante
items.example: We will examine the financial details at a later stage.
items.note: Leaves the later point or phase unspecified, often in a project or process.

items.example: At some point, we will need to replace the old equipment.
items.note: Refers to an unspecified time, usually in the future in this unit.

items.example: For the moment, the temporary solution is working well.
items.note: Means for now, with the expectation that the situation may later change.

items.example: The support engineer called me back straightaway.
items.note: Exercise 61.2 contrasts straightaway with immediate; British English commonly uses straightaway.

units.title: Unit 62 — Condition
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 130–131 (PDF pages 131–132).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Express restrictions and conditions with unless, on condition that, as long as and provided/providing that.
Distinguish in case from in case of and in the event of.
Use supposing and what if to ask about hypothetical future situations.
Form -ever and no matter clauses correctly, using present tense for future conditions.
Use condition-related nouns and formal requirement expressions accurately.

items.example: Unless the engineer approves the change, we cannot restart the machine.
items.note: Means if ... not; do not normally use a second negative to express the same restriction.

items.pt: com a condição de que; desde que
items.example: You may access the laboratory on condition that you complete the safety training.
items.note: Strong and relatively formal; useful for explicit rules and official permissions.

items.example: In case of a power failure, use the emergency lighting.
items.note: Followed by a noun phrase; often appears in warnings, notices and instructions. Not the same as in case + clause.

items.pt: em caso de; na eventualidade de
items.example: In the event of an evacuation, follow the marked exit route.
items.note: Formal alternative to in case of; followed by a noun phrase.

items.example: You can borrow my laptop as long as you return it tonight.
items.note: Common in speech; a relatively relaxed way of setting a condition.

items.example: The equipment may be used so long as the safety guard remains in place.
items.note: Slightly more formal than as long as; less forceful than on condition that.

items.example: The proposal can go ahead provided that the budget is approved.
items.note: More restrictive than as long as, but generally less formal and emphatic than on condition that. The word that can be omitted.

items.example: We can finish by Friday providing that the components arrive today.
items.note: Variant of provided that; the word that is optional. This is a condition, not an ongoing-action use of providing.

items.pt: caso; por precaução; para o caso de
items.example: Save an extra copy in case the computer crashes.
items.note: In case + clause describes a possible event you are preparing for, whether or not it happens.

items.example: Supposing the supplier cancels the order, what should we do?
items.note: Common in conversation for a possible future situation; often more tentative than what if.

items.example: What if we miss the last train home?
items.note: Usually spoken and more direct than supposing; introduces a possible problem or scenario.

items.pt: não importa como; por mais que
items.example: However you arrange the timetable, we will need two shifts.
items.note: Here however means no matter how; do not confuse this use with contrastive however (= nevertheless).

items.pt: qualquer que seja; não importa qual
items.example: Whichever route we choose, we will arrive after dark.
items.note: Means it does not matter which one, among available choices; stress normally falls on ever.

items.pt: onde quer que; não importa onde
items.example: Wherever she works, she keeps detailed technical notes.
items.note: Means no matter where; can introduce a condition-like clause.

items.pt: quem quer que; não importa quem
items.example: Whoever leads the meeting should circulate the agenda first.
items.note: Means no matter who; the verb following whoever agrees with its grammatical subject.

items.pt: o que quer que; não importa o que
items.example: Whatever decision we make, we should document the reasons.
items.note: Means no matter what; featured in the exercise transformations.

items.pt: não importa como; por mais que
items.example: No matter how carefully I check the figures, I sometimes miss a typo.
items.note: Equivalent to however + adjective/adverb/clause in this use; unlike standalone contrastive however.

items.example: No matter which model you select, a calibration step is required.
items.note: Equivalent to whichever in this context.

items.example: No matter where you travel, keep your passport somewhere safe.
items.note: Equivalent to wherever.

items.example: No matter who calls, please ask them to leave a message.
items.note: Equivalent to whoever in this context.

items.pt: não importa o que; aconteça o que acontecer
items.example: No matter what happens, we must follow the safety procedure.
items.note: Equivalent to whatever in conditional clauses.

items.pt: por mais que se esforce; por mais difícil que seja
items.example: However hard we try, we cannot finish without the missing parts.
items.note: However + adjective or adverb can mean no matter how; the exercise also contrasts no matter how hard.

items.example: Certain conditions must be satisfied before the trial can begin.
items.note: Plural noun for requirements that must be fulfilled; also appears in other senses outside this unit.

items.pt: cumprir uma condição; atender a uma exigência
items.example: The applicant must meet every condition before receiving the permit.
items.note: Meet a condition or meet the conditions is a common formal collocation; do not use make a condition for fulfilment.

items.example: Previous programming experience is a prerequisite for this course.
items.note: A condition that is absolutely necessary before something else can happen; rather formal. Often prerequisite for.

items.pt: requisitos de ingresso; critérios de admissão
items.example: The university publishes its entry requirements on the course website.
items.note: Official criteria needed for admission, enrolment or participation; rather formal.

items.pt: em nenhuma circunstância (com negação); sob quaisquer circunstâncias
items.example: We would not disable the alarm under any circumstances.
items.note: Fairly formal; used especially with a negative to mean absolutely never.

items.pt: em quais circunstâncias; em que condições
items.example: Under what circumstances would the company approve remote work?
items.note: Formal question about situations in which something might happen; raised in Exercise 62.4.

items.pt: sob qual condição; com que condição
items.example: On what condition would you agree to share the equipment?
items.note: Asks for a specific required condition, and appears as a speaking target in Exercise 62.4.
